newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian firms eye big role if Iraq oil deal renewed.
newsitem.headline: Russian firms eye big role if Iraq oil deal renewed.

text.p: Russian oil companies are looking to win a major slice of Iraqi crude oil liftings under any new United Nations food-for-oil programme later this year, sources at Russian firms active under the current programme said on Friday.
Russia, a close political ally to Iraq, will probably repeat volumes it plans to lift in the first half of 1997 if a similar $2 billion accord is allowed in the second half, they said.

"If the Iraqi food-for-oil deal is renewed, I would expect to see similar volumes agreed with Russian companies as in the first half of the year, possibly even more," said a source at a major Russian trading company active in Iraqi liftings.

A representive at Zarubezhneft, the Russian trading firm coordinating Russian liftings from Iraq, pegged the total volume Russian companies are set to buy under the first six-month programme at 28.3 to 28.4 million barrels.

Yuri Agababov, deputy chief executive at Zarubezhneft, also said on Thursday that Russian companies had lifted 26.57 million barrels of Iraqi crude by May 15, and that no new deals were likely under the current programme.
Overall oil sales from Iraq are expected to reach 121.56 million barrels, putting Russia's share at 23 percent.
"I think volumes will be around about the same as the quotas we had," said an official at traders MES.

Iraq had eight Russian partners, including trading firms and some of Russia's biggest vertically-integrated oil companies, in the first food-for-oil programme, and a similar list is likely to emerge if the programme is renewed, lifters said.
"I think all eight companies which took part in the first half of the year would be interested in doing so in the future," said a source at one of the trading companies on the list.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, currently visiting Moscow, is to issue a report before June 7 on the accord's effectiveness in alleviating suffering in Iraq. The U.N. Security Council was then to take action on renewing the accord.
Iraq is lobbying for $4 billion in oil sales, around double its current limit, but Russian lifters were working on the assumption that around $2 billion in oil sales would be agreed.
Sources at the lifting companies said conditions had not always been easy during the six month programme.
"Of course the drop in prices has been a very difficult problem," said one official. "It is in the interests of all Russian companies that prices should be higher," he added.
Some traders were bullish for oil demand and prices during the second half of the year.
"I don't think the price drop will affect volumes lifted by Russian companies in any future deal," the official said. "Demand for oil will be high enough around the world."
Another factor which may influence the participation of Russian oil traders, as opposed to producers, in Iraqi oil liftings is a shrinking share of the Russian export market.

Traders' role in Russian oil has come under pressure during the last few months as powerful producers and the Fuel and Energy Ministry have worked to slash exports for state needs, which trading firms have traditionally dominated.
The exports, known as federal programmes, are used to fund state projects such as renovating the Kremlin.
Russian oil analysts say they expect to see the programmes cut further, marginalising traders even more.
"This of course is the biggest nightmare for us," said a trader. "Conditions for traders have definitely become more difficult during the last six months or so."
But he and others put a brave face on the future.

"Traders are still needed. May be we are talking about smaller volumes for traders -- say today we sell 100 tonnes of oil then tomorrow it could be 70 -- but I don't think it's too serious for us," said one Russian dealer.
